title: Categorize Radio Frequencies by Band
condition: Given a list of tactical frequencies and MCRP 3-40.3C.
standard: Categorize each frequency into the correct military radio frequency band (HF, VHF, or UHF) without error per Figure 1-1.
performanceSteps: Identify frequencies between 3 MHz and 30 MHz as High Frequency (HF).
Identify frequencies between 30 MHz and 300 MHz as Very High Frequency (VHF).
Identify frequencies between 300 MHz and 3 GHz as Ultra High Frequency (UHF).

title: Calculate Radio Wavelength
condition: Given a specific operating frequency, the constant for the speed of light, and MCRP 3-40.3C.
standard: Calculate the wavelength (λ) in meters to determine antenna length requirements with 100% accuracy.
performanceSteps: Identify the assigned operating frequency (f).
Identify the velocity of electromagnetic radiation (v) as 300,000,000 meters per second.
Apply the wavelength formula where wavelength equals velocity divided by frequency (λ = v/f).
Express the final wavelength result in meters.

title: Identify Radio Wave Propagation Components
condition: Given a tactical radio system and MCRP 3-40.3C.
standard: Identify the characteristics of radio wave propagation to ensure optimal antenna placement.
performanceSteps: Identify the two components of a radio wave (crest and trough).
Define the wavelength as the distance between successive wave crests.
Determine if the radio wave is propagating as a ground wave (near Earth's surface) or sky wave (radiating skyward).
Identify potential interference factors including natural and manmade noise.

title: Convert Frequency Units
condition: Given a frequency value and MCRP 3-40.3C.
standard: Convert the frequency value between Hertz (Hz), Kilohertz (kHz), Megahertz (MHz), and Gigahertz (GHz) without error.
performanceSteps: Identify the base unit (1 Hz = 1 cycle per second).
Convert to Kilohertz (kHz) by a factor of 1,000.
Convert to Megahertz (MHz) by a factor of 1,000,000.
Convert to Gigahertz (GHz) by a factor of 1,000,000,000.

title: Calculate Antenna Physical Length
condition: Given a target frequency, a calculator, and reference material.
standard: Calculate the physical length of a half-wave or quarter-wave antenna to within 1 percent of the mathematical requirement to ensure resonance at the assigned frequency per MCRP 3-40.3C.
performanceSteps: Identify the assigned operating frequency.
Select the appropriate formula for the antenna type (Half-wave or Quarter-wave).
Calculate the length in feet using the constant 468 (for half-wave) or 234 (for quarter-wave) divided by the frequency in MHz.
Convert the decimal result into feet and inches.
Account for 'end effect' or velocity factor if specific wire types are identified.

title: Construct a Field Expedient Center-Fed Doublet Antenna
condition: Given a radio, transmission line, antenna wire, insulators, support structures, and a target frequency.
standard: Construct and employ the antenna such that a radio link is established with a distant station at the assigned frequency per MCRP 3-40.3C.
performanceSteps: Calculate the required length for each leg of the doublet (quarter-wave each).
Cut two equal lengths of antenna wire.
Attach the wire legs to a center insulator.
Connect the transmission line (coaxial or WD-1/TT) to the center insulator.
Attach end insulators to the wire legs.
Hoist the antenna using supports (masts or trees) to the required height.
Connect the transmission line to the radio set.
Verify the radio link with the distant station.

title: Install an Antenna Grounding System
condition: Given an antenna system, ground rods, counterpoise wire, and hand tools.
standard: Install a grounding system (counterpoise or ground screen) to improve radiation efficiency and ensure operator safety per MCRP 3-40.3C.
performanceSteps: Determine the type of ground required (Ground rod, Counterpoise, or Ground Screen).
Drive ground rods into the earth at the base of the antenna.
Lay out counterpoise radials in a star or circular pattern if soil conductivity is poor.
Ensure all connections between the ground system and the radio/antenna are tight and free of corrosion.
Verify the ground system does not create a trip hazard for personnel.

title: Orient an Antenna for Directionality
condition: Given an erected directional antenna, a compass, and the location of a distant station.
standard: Orient the antenna on the correct azimuth to maximize signal gain and achieve a reliable radio link per MCRP 3-40.3C.
performanceSteps: Determine the grid azimuth to the distant station using a map.
Convert the grid azimuth to a magnetic azimuth.
Identify the antenna's radiation pattern (bidirectional or unidirectional).
Align the major lobe of the antenna's radiation pattern with the calculated azimuth.
Adjust the take-off angle if required for sky wave propagation.
Perform a radio check to confirm maximum signal strength.

title: Perform Field Repair of Wire Antennas
condition: Given a damaged wire antenna system and a field repair kit.
standard: Restore electrical continuity and structural integrity to the antenna to enable communications per MCRP 3-40.3C.
performanceSteps: Identify the location of the break or damage in the wire.
Strip the insulation from the broken ends of the wire.
Join the wires using a Western Union splice or a similar high-strength mechanical connection.
Solder the connection if equipment is available, or wrap with electrical tape to prevent corrosion.
Re-tension the antenna wire to ensure it is clear of the ground and obstructions.
Test the repaired antenna for continuity and resonance.

title: Calculate Antenna Length
condition: Given an operating frequency, a calculator, and writing materials.
standard: Calculate the physical length of a radio antenna to support the assigned frequency to within 1% accuracy using the formulas provided in MCRP 6-22D.
performanceSteps: Identify the assigned operating frequency.
Determine the required antenna type (e.g., half-wave dipole or quarter-wave whip).
Apply the appropriate constant for the unit of measure (feet or meters).
Divide the constant by the frequency to determine the physical length.
Verify the calculated length against the frequency band (HF, VHF, or UHF).

title: Select an Antenna Site
condition: Given a tactical mission, a frequency band (HF, VHF, or UHF), and a designated area of operations.
standard: Select a site that optimizes signal propagation and minimizes interference based on the technical and tactical considerations in MCRP 6-22D.
performanceSteps: Analyze the frequency band requirements (Line of Sight for VHF/UHF vs. Ground/Sky wave for HF).
Evaluate terrain for elevation and obstacles.
Identify potential sources of manmade noise (power lines, engines).
Identify potential sources of natural noise.
Assess ground conductivity for HF operations.
Ensure tactical concealment and doctrinal considerations are met.

title: Determine Antenna Orientation
condition: Given a distant station location, an antenna, and a compass.
standard: Orient the antenna's radiation pattern to achieve maximum signal gain toward the distant station per MCRP 6-22D.
performanceSteps: Determine the azimuth to the distant station.
Identify the antenna's radiation pattern (directional, bidirectional, or omnidirectional).
Align the antenna's primary lobe with the target azimuth.
Select the appropriate polarization (vertical or horizontal) based on the circuit requirement.
Adjust the take-off angle if required for the distance.

title: Construct an Antenna Ground System
condition: Given a radio set, an antenna, and a ground/counterpoise kit or field-expedient wire.
standard: Install a ground or counterpoise system to improve antenna resonance and efficiency in accordance with MCRP 6-22D.
performanceSteps: Evaluate the existing ground conductivity.
Determine the requirement for a counterpoise or ground screen.
Lay out radial wires at the base of the antenna.
Connect the ground system to the radio or antenna base terminal.
Ensure all connections are secure and provide low resistance.

title: Establish an Antenna Farm
condition: Given multiple radio systems, various antenna types, and a designated Command Post (CP) location.
standard: Layout the antenna farm to minimize co-site interference and maximize communication effectiveness per the layout principles in MCRP 6-22D.
performanceSteps: Identify the frequency bands of all active nets.
Determine the polarization requirements for each antenna.
Calculate the minimum separation distance between antennas to prevent interference.
Route power and signal lines to minimize cross-talk and tripping hazards.
Position antennas based on directionality and radiation patterns.
sourceRef: MCRP 6-22D, Chapter 8, Antenna Farm Layout Principles

title: Perform Radio Frequency Unit Conversions
condition: Given a requirement to configure a radio system and a specific frequency expressed in Hertz (Hz), Kilohertz (kHz), Megahertz (MHz), or Gigahertz (GHz).
standard: Convert the frequency to the required unit of measure with 100% accuracy to ensure proper equipment programming per MCRP 3-40.3C.
performanceSteps: Identify the current unit of frequency measurement.
Determine the target unit of frequency measurement required for the radio system.
Apply the conversion factor (1,000 for kHz, 1,000,000 for MHz, 1,000,000,000 for GHz).
Calculate the numerical value for the target unit.
Verify the calculation against the electromagnetic spectrum chart.

title: Calculate Antenna Length
condition: Given an assigned operating frequency, a specific antenna type (half-wave or quarter-wave), and MCRP 3-40.3C.
standard: Calculate the physical length of the antenna required for resonance at the assigned frequency within +/- 1 inch of the mathematical requirement.
performanceSteps: Identify the assigned operating frequency.
Select the appropriate formula for the antenna type (half-wave or quarter-wave).
Calculate the wavelength based on the speed of light (300 million meters per second).
Determine the physical length in feet or meters.
Account for velocity factor if applicable to the specific wire type.

title: Orient an Antenna for Directional Transmission
condition: Given a tactical radio, a directional antenna, a lensatic compass, and the location of a distant station.
standard: Orient the antenna on the correct azimuth to achieve maximum signal strength and establish a reliable communication link per MCRP 3-40.3C.
performanceSteps: Determine the azimuth to the distant station using a map or provided coordinates.
Identify the antenna's radiation pattern (directionality).
Determine the required polarization (vertical or horizontal) based on the distant station's configuration.
Align the antenna's primary lobe toward the distant station using a lensatic compass.
Adjust the take-off angle if required for atmospheric conditions.
Perform a radio check to verify signal strength.

title: Construct an Antenna Grounding System
condition: Given an antenna system, a grounding kit or field-expedient materials, and a designated site.
standard: Install a ground or counterpoise system to ensure antenna resonance and operator safety per MCRP 3-40.3C.
performanceSteps: Assess the soil conductivity at the antenna site.
Select the appropriate grounding method (ground rod, counterpoise, or ground screen).
Drive the ground rod into the earth or deploy counterpoise radials in a symmetrical pattern.
Connect the ground lead to the antenna's ground terminal.
Ensure all connections are tight and free of corrosion.
Verify the reduction of stray RF and improvement in signal stability.

title: Assemble an OE-254 Antenna
condition: Given an OE-254 antenna kit, a designated site, and a requirement to establish VHF communications.
standard: To ensure the antenna is assembled and erected according to technical specifications, providing maximum gain and directivity for the assigned frequency, per MCRP 3-40.3C.
performanceSteps: Inventory all OE-254 components for completeness and serviceability.
Assemble the mast sections to the required height.
Attach the radiator elements to the antenna head.
Connect the transmission line (coaxial cable) to the antenna base.
Erect the antenna mast using the base plate and guy ropes.
Secure the guy lines to stakes at the appropriate distance to ensure stability.
Verify vertical polarization and clear line-of-sight where possible.

title: Select VHF/UHF Antennas Based on Environmental Factors
condition: Given a mission requirement, a specific frequency range (VHF/UHF), and a tactical environment (e.g., vegetated area, vehicle interior).
standard: Select the antenna type that maximizes signal strength and minimizes interference (multipath or noise) according to the characteristics of the operating area.
performanceSteps: Identify the required frequency range (VHF or UHF).
Determine the required polarization (Vertical or Horizontal).
Analyze the environment for potential interference (e.g., vegetated areas, multipath interference).
Select the appropriate radiator type (Vertical Whip, OE-254, or Cross Section Radiator).
Determine if a dual-function antenna is required for simultaneous VHF/UHF operations.
Position the antenna to mitigate noise and interference from nearby sources.

title: Establish HF Sky Wave Communications
condition: Given an HF radio set, a distant station, and ionospheric data (MUF/LUF).
standard: Establish a reliable communication link by selecting a frequency between the Maximum Usable Frequency (MUF) and Lowest Useful Frequency (LUF) and adjusting the antenna for the correct angle of incidence.
performanceSteps: Determine the MUF and LUF for the intended transmission path and time of day.
Select an operating frequency that is below the MUF but above the LUF to ensure reflection and override noise.
Calculate the required skip distance based on the receiver location.
Adjust the antenna height to control the angle of incidence (lower height for NVIS/higher angle; higher height for long-distance/lower angle).
Monitor for fading (periodic signal strength changes) and adjust frequency or antenna orientation if necessary.
Account for irregular ionospheric variations (Sporadic E, SID, or Ionospheric Storms) during link maintenance.

title: Orient Directional Antennas to Mitigate Interference
condition: Given a horizontal half-wave antenna, a desired signal source, and an identified interfering station.
standard: Orient the antenna to maximize the signal-to-noise ratio by placing the interfering source in the antenna's null and the desired source in the antenna's broadside.
performanceSteps: Identify the direction of the desired signal source.
Identify the direction of the interfering signal or noise source.
Position the horizontal half-wave antenna so the broadside (perpendicular to the wire) faces the desired station.
Rotate the antenna so that the ends (nulls) point toward the interfering station.
Verify the reduction of interference and the clarity of the desired signal.
Adjust antenna height to further refine the radiation pattern if interference persists.

title: Calculate Antenna Length
condition: Given a specific operating frequency, a calculator, and reference material.
standard: Determine the physical length of the antenna wire to within one inch of the mathematical requirement based on the formula for a half-wave or quarter-wave antenna.
performanceSteps: Identify the assigned operating frequency.
Select the appropriate formula for the antenna type (e.g., 468 / frequency in MHz for half-wave).
Calculate the physical length of the radiating element.
Calculate the length of the counterpoise or ground radials if required.
Measure the wire to the calculated length.

title: Construct an Antenna Grounding System
condition: Given a radio set, antenna, grounding rod, and counterpoise or ground screen materials.
standard: Establish a low-resistance path to earth to improve radiation efficiency and ensure operator safety.
performanceSteps: Select a site with moist soil if available to improve conductivity.
Drive the ground rod into the earth at a 90-degree angle.
Connect the equipment ground terminal to the ground rod using a low-impedance conductor.
Deploy counterpoise radials or a ground screen in a star or grid pattern if soil conductivity is poor.
Ensure all connections are tight and free of corrosion.

title: Orient an Antenna for Maximum Signal Strength
condition: Given a directional antenna, a compass, and the grid coordinates of a distant station.
standard: Align the antenna's major radiation lobe with the distant station's azimuth within +/- 5 degrees.
performanceSteps: Determine the grid azimuth to the distant station.
Convert the grid azimuth to a magnetic azimuth using the G-M angle.
Identify the antenna's radiation pattern (directional or bi-directional).
Physically align the antenna's radiating element or boom toward the distant station using a compass.
Verify signal strength with the distant station and adjust for maximum gain.

title: Construct an AS-2259/GR Antenna
condition: Given an AS-2259/GR antenna kit and a designated site.
standard: Assemble and erect the antenna to support Near Vertical Incidence Skywave (NVIS) communications.
performanceSteps: Inventory all antenna components (mast sections, radiating elements, base).
Assemble the mast sections to the required height.
Attach the radiating elements and guy lines to the top of the mast.
Erect the mast and secure it using the guy lines and stakes.
Connect the RF cable to the radio and the antenna feed point.
Verify the VSWR (Voltage Standing Wave Ratio) is within acceptable limits.

title: Construct an OE-254 Antenna
condition: Given an OE-254 antenna kit and a designated site.
standard: Assemble and erect the antenna to support VHF line-of-sight communications.
performanceSteps: Inventory all components including the feed cone, elements, and mast sections.
Assemble the feed cone and attach the radiating elements.
Assemble the mast sections and attach the feed cone assembly to the top.
Erect the mast while maintaining tension on the guy ropes.
Secure the guy ropes to the stakes at 120-degree intervals.
Connect the RF cable to the antenna and the radio set.

title: Site an Antenna Farm
condition: Given a mission, a list of communication nets, and a tactical area of responsibility.
standard: Select and layout an antenna site that minimizes mutual interference and maximizes signal propagation.
performanceSteps: Analyze the terrain for elevation and clear lines of sight.
Determine the required separation distance between antennas to prevent cosite interference.
Identify the polarization requirements (vertical or horizontal) for each net.
Layout antenna positions based on frequency band and directionality.
Plan the routing of power and signal lines to prevent tripping hazards and interference.
Ensure the site meets tactical concealment and security requirements.

title: Calculate Antenna Length
condition: Given a specific operating frequency, a calculator, and writing materials.
standard: Calculate the physical length of a half-wave dipole or quarter-wave vertical antenna to within +/- 1 inch of the mathematical requirement based on the formula provided in the reference.
performanceSteps: Identify the operating frequency in Megahertz (MHz).
Select the appropriate formula for the antenna type (e.g., 468 / frequency for a half-wave dipole in feet).
Perform the mathematical calculation to determine total length.
Divide the total length by two for individual dipole elements if required.
Convert decimal feet to inches for physical measurement.

title: Construct a Half-Wave Dipole Antenna
condition: Given a radio, transmission line (coaxial cable), antenna wire, insulators, and a calculated frequency.
standard: Construct and employ the antenna so that it is resonant at the assigned frequency and capable of establishing communications with a distant station.
performanceSteps: Measure and cut two equal lengths of antenna wire based on the calculated frequency.
Attach the wire elements to a center insulator.
Connect the transmission line (coaxial cable) to the center insulator.
Attach end insulators to the wire elements.
Secure the antenna to supports (trees or poles) at the required height and orientation.
Connect the transmission line to the radio equipment.
Perform a radio check to verify signal strength.

title: Employ AS-2259/GR Antenna
condition: Given an AS-2259/GR antenna kit, an HF radio, and a designated site.
standard: Assemble and erect the antenna to support Near Vertical Incidence Skywave (NVIS) communications as per the technical manual.
performanceSteps: Inventory all antenna components (mast sections, top cap, radiators, stakes).
Assemble the mast sections on the base plate.
Attach the top cap and the four wire radiators.
Erect the mast while deploying the radiators as guy wires.
Secure the radiators to the ground using stakes at 90-degree intervals.
Connect the RF cable to the radio.
Tune the radio to the assigned frequency.

title: Employ OE-254 Antenna
condition: Given an OE-254 antenna kit, a VHF radio, and a designated site.
standard: Assemble and erect the antenna to its full height (30 feet) to establish VHF line-of-sight communications.
performanceSteps: Inventory the OE-254 kit components.
Assemble the antenna head (radiating elements).
Connect the RF cable to the antenna head.
Assemble the mast sections.
Attach the antenna head to the top mast section.
Attach guy ropes to the mast at the designated points.
Raise the mast and secure guy ropes to ground stakes.
Connect the RF cable to the VHF radio.

title: Construct an Antenna Ground System
condition: Given a vertical whip antenna, ground stakes, and copper wire (counterpoise).
standard: Install a ground screen or counterpoise to improve the radiation efficiency of the antenna system.
performanceSteps: Identify the soil type to determine ground conductivity.
Drive a ground rod into the earth near the antenna base.
Lay out radial wires (counterpoise) extending from the antenna base.
Ensure radials are at least 1/4 wavelength of the operating frequency.
Connect all radials and the ground rod to the radio's ground terminal or antenna base.
Verify the reduction in ground resistance or improvement in signal.

title: Orient Antenna for Maximum Signal Strength
condition: Given an erected directional antenna and a distant station's location.
standard: Orient the antenna's major lobe toward the receiving station to achieve maximum gain.
performanceSteps: Determine the azimuth to the distant station using a map and compass.
Identify the radiation pattern (polarization and directionality) of the specific antenna in use.
Physically rotate or adjust the antenna elements to align with the determined azimuth.
Adjust the take-off angle if using an HF antenna for skywave propagation.
Coordinate with the distant station to confirm peak signal strength.

title: Select an HF Antenna
condition: Given a mission requirement, a specific frequency, a distance to the distant station, and MCRP 6-22D.
standard: Select the antenna type that optimizes gain and propagation (Groundwave, Skywave, or NVIS) for the required distance and frequency in accordance with MCRP 6-22D Chapter 4.
performanceSteps: Determine the distance to the distant station.
Identify the required propagation mode (NVIS, Long-range Skywave, or Groundwave).
Determine the required antenna gain based on mission requirements.
Evaluate site constraints (available space, terrain, and vegetation).
Select the appropriate HF antenna (e.g., AS-2259/GR, Half-Wave Dipole, Inverted Vee, or Long Wire) based on the selection procedure in MCRP 6-22D.

title: Install an AS-2259/GR Antenna
condition: Given an AS-2259/GR antenna kit, an HF radio set, and MCRP 6-22D.
standard: Assemble and erect the antenna to provide Near Vertical Incidence Skywave (NVIS) communications, ensuring all connections are secure and the mast is stable, per MCRP 6-22D Section 4-9.
performanceSteps: Inventory all antenna components.
Assemble the mast sections to the required height.
Attach the radiating elements and top assembly.
Secure the guy lines and anchors to stabilize the mast.
Connect the transmission line to the antenna base and the radio set.
Verify the antenna is configured for NVIS propagation.

title: Install an OE-254 Antenna
condition: Given an OE-254 antenna kit, a VHF radio set, and MCRP 6-22D.
standard: Assemble and erect the antenna to provide VHF line-of-sight communications, ensuring the mast is vertical and guy lines are tensioned, per MCRP 6-22D Section 5-10.
performanceSteps: Inventory all OE-254 components.
Assemble the mast sections on the ground.
Attach the feed cone and radiating elements.
Connect the coaxial transmission line to the feed cone.
Erect the mast assembly to a vertical position.
Secure guy ropes to stakes at 120-degree intervals.
Connect the coaxial cable to the radio set.

title: Site an Antenna Farm
condition: Given a tactical scenario, multiple radio systems (HF, VHF, UHF), and MCRP 6-22D.
standard: Determine the optimal placement for multiple antennas to minimize interference and maximize signal effectiveness based on tactical and technical considerations in MCRP 6-22D Chapter 8.
performanceSteps: Identify the command post type (Tactical, Main, or Rear).
Evaluate tactical considerations (concealment, security, and accessibility).
Evaluate technical considerations (terrain, soil conductivity, and man-made interference).
Determine the internal arrangement based on frequency bands to prevent co-site interference.
Select antenna polarization (vertical or horizontal) based on the net requirements.
Plan the layout of power and signal lines to avoid interference and tripping hazards.
Establish separation distances between transmitting and receiving antennas.

title: Construct a Half-Wave Dipole Antenna
condition: Given a frequency, wire, insulators, a transmission line, and MCRP 6-22D.
standard: Calculate the required length and construct the antenna to support HF communications for the assigned frequency per MCRP 6-22D Section 4-14.
performanceSteps: Calculate the length of the half-wave radiator using the formula (468 / Frequency in MHz).
Cut the wire into two equal quarter-wave sections.
Attach the wire sections to the center insulator.
Attach end insulators to the wire sections.
Connect the transmission line (coaxial or balanced) to the center insulator.
Measure and adjust the antenna height and orientation for the desired propagation.

title: Calculate Antenna Length
condition: Given a specific operating frequency and a requirement to construct a wire antenna.
standard: Calculate the physical length of the antenna elements to within 1% of the theoretical requirement based on the formula provided in the reference.
performanceSteps: Identify the target operating frequency.
Select the appropriate formula for the antenna type (e.g., half-wave or quarter-wave).
Calculate the length in feet or meters.
Adjust for velocity factor if applicable.
Verify the calculated length against the frequency band limits.

title: Install an AS-2259/GR Antenna
condition: Given an AS-2259/GR antenna kit, a designated site, and a requirement to establish Near Vertical Incidence Skywave (NVIS) communications.
standard: Assemble and erect the antenna so that it is structurally sound and provides a signal capable of supporting communications, in accordance with the technical manual.
performanceSteps: Inventory all antenna components.
Assemble the mast sections.
Attach the top and bottom radiator elements.
Secure the guy ropes and stakes.
Connect the transmission line to the radio set.
Verify the antenna is oriented for NVIS propagation.

title: Install an OE-254 Antenna
condition: Given an OE-254 antenna kit and a requirement to provide VHF line-of-sight communications.
standard: Erect the antenna to its full height and secure it to withstand environmental conditions while maintaining a clear line of sight to the receiving station.
performanceSteps: Assemble the antenna base and radiator elements.
Connect the RF cable to the base assembly.
Raise the mast sections sequentially.
Deploy and secure guy wires at the appropriate intervals.
Ensure the antenna is vertically polarized.
Perform a radio check to verify operation.

title: Construct a Field Expedient Wire Antenna
condition: Given field wire (WD-1/TT), insulators, a radio set, and a requirement to establish communications when standard antennas are unavailable.
standard: Construct a functional antenna (such as a Half-Wave Dipole or Inverted Vee) that achieves resonance at the assigned frequency and enables communication.
performanceSteps: Determine the required antenna type based on the mission and terrain.
Calculate the length of the wire elements for the assigned frequency.
Cut the wire to the calculated length, allowing for terminal connections.
Attach insulators to the ends and the center feed point.
Connect the transmission line (feed line) to the center point.
Erect the antenna using available supports (trees, poles, etc.).
Orient the antenna for maximum directivity toward the distant station.

title: Perform Field Repair of Antennas
condition: Given a damaged antenna (whip or wire) and a field repair kit.
standard: Restore the electrical continuity and structural integrity of the antenna to allow for immediate resumption of communications.
performanceSteps: Identify the point of failure or break in the antenna or transmission line.
Strip insulation from wire ends if repairing a wire antenna.
Splice the broken ends using a Western Union splice or similar secure connection.
Seal the connection with electrical tape or weatherproofing material.
Repair broken whip sections using a splint or emergency sleeve.
Test the antenna for electrical continuity and signal strength.

title: Fabricate a Field-Expedient Ground Connection
condition: Given a radio system requiring a ground, a pipe or conduit to serve as a ground rod, ground wire, ground clamp, cleaning materials (sandpaper or scraper), and tape.
standard: To establish a low-resistance connection that supports radio wave radiation and prevents oxidation, ensuring the installation does not contaminate nearby drinking water supplies per MCRP 3-40.3C.
performanceSteps: Identify a location for the ground rod away from nearby drinking water supplies.
Fabricate a ground rod from available pipe or conduit.
Clean the ground rod thoroughly by scraping and sandpapering at the point of connection.
Install a clean ground clamp onto the prepared section of the rod.
Solder or join the ground wire to the ground clamp.
Cover the joint with tape to prevent an increase in resistance due to oxidation.

title: Install an Antenna Counterpoise
condition: Given an antenna system, wire, and insulators, in an environment where a direct ground connection is impractical due to high soil resistance.
standard: To provide an artificial ground that produces the required radiation pattern, ensuring the counterpoise is insulated from the ground and sized correctly per MCRP 3-40.3C.
performanceSteps: Determine the required size of the counterpoise (must be at least equal to or larger than the size of the antenna).
Erect the wire counterpoise a short distance above the ground.
Insulate the counterpoise from the ground using insulators.
Arrange the counterpoise in a simple geometric pattern if the antenna is mounted vertically.
Connect the counterpoise to the radio system ground terminal.

title: Determine Antenna Polarization Requirements
condition: Given a communication mission, a specified frequency band (LF, MF, HF, VHF, or UHF), and tactical antennas.
standard: To optimize signal strength and radiation patterns based on frequency and transmission type (ground wave vs. sky wave) per MCRP 3-40.3C.
performanceSteps: Identify the operating frequency band and transmission mode (ground wave or sky wave).
Select vertical polarization for medium and low frequency ground wave transmissions to minimize ground loss.
Select horizontal polarization for HF sky wave transmission to utilize high-angle radiation and directional properties.
Match the polarization of the transmitting and receiving antennas for VHF or UHF line-of-sight communications.
Employ circular polarization for satellite communications by combining equal magnitudes of vertical and horizontal waves with a 90-degree phase difference.

title: Calculate Antenna Length
condition: Given a specific operating frequency, a requirement for a half-wave or quarter-wave antenna, and reference material.
standard: Calculate the physical length of the antenna wire to ensure resonance at the assigned frequency, in accordance with MCRP 3-40.3C Section III.
performanceSteps: Identify the assigned operating frequency.
Determine the required antenna type (half-wave or quarter-wave).
Apply the standard formula for antenna length calculation (468/frequency for half-wave in feet).
Account for velocity factor and end effects if applicable.
Measure and cut the antenna wire to the calculated length.

title: Orient Antenna for Maximum Signal Strength
condition: Given a tactical radio, an antenna system, and the location of a distant station.
standard: Orient the antenna to achieve the highest possible signal-to-noise (S/N) ratio and proper polarization to establish a reliable communications circuit.
performanceSteps: Determine the azimuth to the distant receiving station.
Identify the required polarization (vertical or horizontal) based on the frequency band and distance.
Align the antenna's radiation pattern toward the receiving station.
Adjust the take-off angle based on the required propagation path (Ground Wave vs. Sky Wave).
Verify signal strength and adjust orientation for maximum S/N ratio.

title: Install an Antenna Grounding System
condition: Given a radio set, an antenna, and grounding materials (ground stakes, wire, or counterpoise kit).
standard: Install a ground screen or counterpoise to improve antenna efficiency and radiation characteristics per MCRP 3-40.3C Section II.
performanceSteps: Assess the Earth's electrical characteristics and conductivity at the site.
Select the appropriate grounding method (grounded antenna, counterpoise, or ground screen).
Drive ground stakes or lay out counterpoise radials in the required pattern.
Connect the grounding system to the radio's ground terminal.
Ensure all connections are tight and provide low resistance to the Earth.

title: Select Frequency Band for Propagation Path
condition: Given a mission requirement, distance to the distant station, and Table 1-1 (Frequency Range Characteristics).
standard: Select the appropriate frequency band (HF, VHF, or UHF) and propagation mode (Ground Wave or Sky Wave) to maintain a continuous link.
performanceSteps: Determine the distance to the receiving station.
Analyze the terrain for Line of Sight (LOS) obstructions.
Select HF for long-range sky wave (100-8000 miles) or VHF/UHF for short-range LOS (0-50 miles).
Identify the Maximum Usable Frequency (MUF) for sky wave paths.
Select the frequency that provides the most direct path with minimal fading.

title: Configure Antenna for Near-Vertical Incidence Skywave (NVIS)
condition: Given an HF radio set, a wire antenna, and a requirement to communicate within a skip zone.
standard: Adjust the antenna height and configuration to achieve a high angle of incidence for NVIS propagation, ensuring signal return within the skip zone.
performanceSteps: Identify the boundaries of the skip zone where ground wave is unusable.
Lower the antenna height to increase the angle of radiation (angle of incidence).
Select a frequency below the MUF that supports NVIS.
Orient the antenna to provide a broad, even signal pattern directly upward.
Establish communication with the station located within the skip zone.

title: Ground an Antenna System
condition: Given a tactical radio, antenna, grounding stake, and mallet in a field environment.
standard: To ensure maximum power radiation by minimizing ground resistance and preventing transmitter power dissipation as heat, ensuring the grounding stake is driven approximately one meter into the earth per MCRP 3-40.3C.
performanceSteps: Identify the antenna feed point.
Select a location for the ground connection near the antenna base.
Drive the grounding stake approximately one meter into the earth to ensure average conductivity.
Connect the antenna ground lead to the grounding stake.
Verify the connection is secure to prevent power loss through heat dissipation.

title: Mitigate Manmade Noise Interference
condition: Given a tactical radio system experiencing interference in an environment with manmade noise sources (e.g., power lines, vehicles, or electric motors).
standard: To improve the signal-to-noise ratio by exploiting wave characteristics and physical placement to reject interfering signals per MCRP 3-40.3C.
performanceSteps: Identify potential manmade noise sources in the immediate vicinity.
Reorient the receiving antenna to horizontal polarization to reduce reception of vertically polarized noise waves.
Relocate the receiving system at least one kilometer away from busy streets or highways if interference persists.
Utilize a narrowband antenna to reject strong interfering signals near the desired frequency.
Ensure the antenna and transmission line are balanced with respect to the ground to cancel noise voltages.

title: Construct an Artificial Ground (Counterpoise)
condition: Given a vertical whip or monopole antenna, conductive material, and a tactical radio in an area with poor soil conductivity.
standard: To provide an artificial ground that minimizes impedance and ensures maximum current flow for radiation per MCRP 3-40.3C.
performanceSteps: Determine the requirement for an artificial ground based on soil conductivity and antenna performance.
Select appropriate conductive material for the counterpoise.
Connect the counterpoise to the antenna's ground terminal at the feed point.
Deploy the counterpoise radials or mesh to create a reflective ground plane.
Verify the antenna is resonated to ensure impedance is pure resistance.

title: Install Antenna Transmission Lines
condition: Given a transceiver, antenna, transmission line, and necessary connectors/baluns.
standard: To connect the transceiver to the antenna while minimizing energy loss and matching impedance per MCRP 3-40.3C.
performanceSteps: Select the appropriate transmission line type for the frequency and equipment.
Inspect cable connectors for physical damage or debris.
Connect the transmission line to the transceiver output.
Connect the transmission line to the antenna feed point.
Install a balun if connecting an unbalanced transmission line to a balanced antenna.
Optimize line length to minimize attenuation and energy loss.

title: Employ an AS-2259/GR Antenna
condition: Given an HF radio, AS-2259/GR antenna kit, and a mission requirement.
standard: Assemble and orient the antenna to establish HF Near Vertical Incidence Skywave (NVIS) communications per MCRP 6-22D.
performanceSteps: Inventory all AS-2259/GR antenna components.
Assemble the mast sections to the required height.
Attach the top cap and radiator elements.
Erect the mast assembly safely.
Secure the guy lines and ground stakes.
Connect the RF cable to the radio and the antenna base.
Verify signal strength and communication link.

title: Employ an OE-254 Antenna
condition: Given a VHF radio, OE-254 antenna kit, and a mission requirement.
standard: Assemble and erect the antenna to establish VHF line-of-sight (LOS) communications per MCRP 6-22D.
performanceSteps: Inventory all OE-254 antenna components.
Assemble the feedcone and radiator elements.
Connect the coaxial cable to the feedcone assembly.
Assemble mast sections and attach the antenna head.
Erect the mast to the vertical position.
Secure the mast using guy lines and stakes.
Route the coaxial cable to the radio equipment.

title: Site an Antenna Farm
condition: Given a tactical scenario, unit location, and CIS requirements.
standard: Select a location for the antenna farm that accounts for tactical, technical, and doctrinal considerations per MCRP 6-22D.
performanceSteps: Identify the type of command post (Main, Rear, or Tactical).
Evaluate terrain for Line of Sight (LOS) and NVIS requirements.
Analyze the site for potential interference (noise, multipath, or vegetated areas).
Determine the internal arrangement based on frequency bands and polarization.
Plan the layout for power and signal lines to minimize interference.
Ensure the site supports tactical requirements for concealment and security.

title: Construct a Half-Wave Dipole Antenna
condition: Given an HF radio, antenna wire, insulators, coaxial cable, and an assigned frequency.
standard: Calculate the required length and construct the antenna to support HF communications at the assigned frequency per MCRP 6-22D.
performanceSteps: Calculate the length of the antenna elements based on the assigned frequency.
Cut the antenna wire to the calculated dimensions.
Attach the center insulator and connect the feedline.
Attach end insulators to the radiator wires.
Deploy the antenna at the required height and orientation (horizontal or inverted vee).
Connect the feedline to the radio and verify the Standing Wave Ratio (SWR).

title: Establish Communications using Reflected Waves
condition: Given a VHF/UHF radio and a scenario where direct Line of Sight (LOS) is obstructed by terrain or structures.
standard: Direct antennas toward a reflecting object to achieve practical communications per MCRP 6-22D.
performanceSteps: Identify a suitable reflecting structure (tall building, mountain, or water tower) visible to both stations.
Direct the transmitting antenna toward the point of maximum reflection.
Direct the receiving antenna toward the same reflecting point.
Adjust polarization (vertical or horizontal) to maximize signal strength.
Verify signal amplitude and phase to ensure constructive combination of waves.

title: Select an HF Antenna for Sky Wave Propagation
condition: Given a mission requirement, a circuit distance, time of day, and MCRP 3-40.3C.
standard: Select an antenna that meets the required take-off angle and coverage requirements for the specified distance and time of day per Table 4-1.
performanceSteps: Determine the circuit (range) distance.
Identify the required take-off angle based on time of day (Daytime vs Nighttime) using Table 4-1.
Determine the required coverage (omnidirectional, bidirectional, or directional) based on station locations.
Examine available construction materials and supports.
Evaluate the proposed antenna site for physical space constraints.
Select the specific antenna type that matches the propagation and site requirements.

title: Construct a Field Expedient Antenna
condition: Given a radio set, assigned frequency, wire, insulators, supports, and MCRP 3-40.3C.
standard: Construct the antenna to the calculated length for the assigned frequency, ensuring it is properly insulated and oriented to establish communication.
performanceSteps: Determine the antenna type required (e.g., End-Fed Half-Wave or Center-Fed Doublet).
Calculate the physical length of the antenna wire based on the assigned frequency.
Cut the antenna wire to the calculated length.
Attach insulators to the antenna wire ends and feed point.
Connect the transmission line to the antenna.
Erect the antenna using available supports (masts or vegetation).
Ensure the antenna is not in close proximity to objects that cause detrimental scattering or re-radiation.

title: Perform Field Repair of Antenna Components
condition: Given a damaged antenna system (whip, wire, guys, or masts), repair materials, and MCRP 3-40.3C.
standard: Restore the antenna system to an operational state ensuring electrical continuity and structural stability.
performanceSteps: Identify the point of failure (whip, wire, guy, or mast).
Clean the contact points of the damaged components to ensure good electrical conductivity.
Splice or bridge broken wire or whip sections.
Repair or replace damaged guy lines to maintain structural tension.
Repair or reinforce damaged mast sections.
Verify the repair by checking for electrical continuity and signal reception.

title: Install Transmission Lines
condition: Given a radio transmitter, an antenna, various transmission lines (coaxial or twin-lead), and MCRP 3-40.3C.
standard: Select and install a transmission line that matches the impedance of the system and minimizes attenuation loss.
performanceSteps: Identify the impedance of the transmitter and the antenna.
Select the largest diameter transmission line available that matches the system impedance.
Inspect the insulation material (dielectric) for suitability based on the operating frequency.
Route the transmission line to minimize length and avoid sharp bends.
Connect the transmission line to the antenna and transmitter ensuring tight, clean connections.
Protect the transmission line from environmental damage or interference.

title: Calculate Physical Length of a Field Expedient Antenna
condition: Given an assigned frequency between 3 and 50 MHz, a calculator, and MCRP 3-40.3C.
standard: Calculate the physical length of a half-wave or long-wire antenna in feet or meters to within +/- 1% accuracy of the formula results.
performanceSteps: Identify the assigned operating frequency in MHz.
Determine the antenna type (Half-wave or Long-wire).
Select the appropriate formula for the unit of measure (Meters: 142.5 / Freq; Feet: 468 / Freq).
Apply the 0.95 correction factor for end effect/velocity reduction.
Calculate the total physical length for a half-wave antenna.
Calculate the length for a long-wire antenna using the harmonic operation formula [Length (m) = 150 (N - 0.05) / Freq] if required.

title: Construct a Field Expedient Ground
condition: Given a tactical radio, antenna system, ground rods or bayonets, and soil treatment materials (salts/water).
standard: Establish a ground connection that provides the maximum possible conductivity and least resistance to ground to support antenna radiation.
performanceSteps: Identify the ground type required (rod, metal structure, or underground pipe).
Drive metal rods or bayonets into the soil to the maximum depth possible.
Connect ground leads to the grounding device ensuring a tight, metal-to-metal connection.
Assess soil conductivity based on moisture and soil type.
Treat soil with conductive substances (sodium chloride, calcium chloride, or magnesium sulfate) in solution if resistance is high.
Ensure the ground lead is as short as possible to minimize ground losses.

title: Construct a Center-Fed Doublet Antenna
condition: Given a specific frequency, field wire (WD-1/TT), insulators, a transmission line, and MCRP 3-40.3C.
standard: Construct and erect a center-fed doublet antenna cut to the correct physical length for the assigned frequency to enable HF communications.
performanceSteps: Calculate the total physical length of the antenna for the assigned frequency.
Cut the wire into two equal halves (each a quarter-wavelength).
Attach a center insulator to join the two wire halves.
Connect the transmission line (e.g., 300-ohm twin lead or 50-ohm coax) to the center terminals.
Attach end insulators to both ends of the antenna wire.
Erect the antenna using masts or field expedients (trees/poles).
Adjust antenna height and orientation for optimal signal radiation.

title: Optimize Transmission Line Length
condition: Given a transceiver with 50-ohm impedance, a transmission line with mismatched impedance, and a single operating frequency.
standard: Cut the transmission line to a specific length to match the antenna impedance to the transmitter using standing wave repetitions.
performanceSteps: Determine the impedance of the transceiver (typically 50 ohms).
Identify the impedance of the available transmission line.
Calculate the electrical half-wavelength for the operating frequency.
Cut the transmission line to a length that is an exact multiple of a half-wavelength to repeat the receiver impedance at the antenna.
For end-fed long-wire antennas, calculate and cut a quarter-wavelength matching section if required.
Connect the optimized line between the radio and the antenna.

title: Employ Reflected Waves for LOS Communication
condition: Given a Line of Sight (LOS) path obstructed by terrain or structures, and directional antennas.
standard: Orient antennas to exploit reflecting surfaces to achieve communication beyond normal LOS distances.
performanceSteps: Identify a suitable reflecting surface (tall building, mountain, or water tower) visible to both stations.
Direct the transmitting antenna toward the point of maximum reflection on the object.
Direct the receiving antenna toward the same point of reflection.
Select vertical polarization to minimize phase difference between direct and reflected waves.
Adjust antenna aim to maximize signal strength (constructive interference).

title: Calculate Antenna Length for a Specific Frequency
condition: Given a target frequency, a calculator, and MCRP 3-40.3C.
standard: Calculate the physical length of a half-wave dipole antenna in feet to within +/- 1 inch of the mathematical requirement based on the formula 468 / Frequency (MHz).
performanceSteps: Identify the assigned operating frequency in Megahertz (MHz).
Select the appropriate formula for a half-wave dipole (468 / Frequency).
Divide 468 by the operating frequency to determine the total length in feet.
Divide the total length by two to determine the length of each individual element (leg).
Convert decimal feet to inches for precise measurement.

title: Construct a Half-Wave Dipole Antenna
condition: Given a radio set, antenna wire, insulators, a transmission line (coaxial cable), and a measuring tape.
standard: Construct the antenna to the calculated frequency length so that it is capable of radiating a signal at the assigned frequency with a proper impedance match.
performanceSteps: Calculate the required length for the assigned frequency.
Measure and cut two equal lengths of antenna wire.
Attach the wire elements to a center insulator.
Connect the transmission line (coax) to the center insulator, ensuring the center conductor and shield are connected to opposite elements.
Attach end insulators to the extremities of the wire elements.
Secure the antenna to supports (trees or poles) at the required height and orientation.

title: Employ an AS-2259/GR Antenna
condition: Given an AS-2259/GR antenna kit, a radio set, and a designated site.
standard: Erect the antenna to support Near Vertical Incidence Skywave (NVIS) communications, ensuring all mast sections are seated and guy wires are properly tensioned.
performanceSteps: Inventory all components of the AS-2259/GR kit.
Assemble the mast sections by sliding them together.
Attach the top cap assembly and the four whip elements.
Connect the RF cable to the base of the antenna.
Raise the mast vertically while deploying the four radiating elements as guy wires.
Secure the radiating elements to the ground using stakes at 90-degree intervals.
Connect the antenna to the radio set and verify the communication link.

title: Employ an OE-254 Antenna
condition: Given an OE-254/GR antenna kit, a VHF radio set, and a designated site.
standard: Assemble and erect the antenna to its full height (30 feet) to support VHF line-of-sight communications.
performanceSteps: Layout the antenna components and inspect for damage.
Assemble the feedcone and attach the three upper and three lower radiating elements.
Attach the feedcone to the top mast section.
Connect the coaxial cable to the feedcone.
Assemble the mast sections while raising the antenna.
Deploy and secure the guy ropes at the 15-foot and 30-foot levels.
Ensure the mast is vertical and the base plate is stable.
Connect the cable to the radio and perform a radio check.

title: Perform Field Repair of a Whip Antenna
condition: Given a damaged or broken whip antenna and field expedient materials (wire, tape, splinting material).
standard: Restore electrical continuity to the antenna to allow for emergency transmissions.
performanceSteps: Identify the point of the break or damage.
Clean the area around the break to ensure good metal-to-metal contact.
Overlap the broken sections or use a conductive splint (e.g., a piece of wire or metal rod).
Secure the repair with tape or wire ties to maintain mechanical stability.
Verify electrical continuity using a multimeter or by observing a reduction in SWR (if equipment is available).

title: Construct a Field Expedient Vertical Half-Rhombic Antenna
condition: Given antenna wire, a terminating resistor (approx. 500-600 ohms), an insulator, a mast or support, and a target azimuth.
standard: Construct and orient the antenna toward the distant station to provide directional gain in the HF band.
performanceSteps: Determine the azimuth to the distant station.
Calculate the length of the wire based on the desired frequency (typically 2 to 4 wavelengths).
Attach one end of the wire to the radio (feed point).
Run the wire to the top of a central support (mast) and through an insulator.
Slope the wire down toward the ground in the direction of the distant station.
Connect the end of the wire to a terminating resistor.
Connect the other side of the resistor to a ground stake.
Ensure the antenna is aligned within 5 degrees of the target azimuth.

title: Orient Antenna for Polarization
condition: Given a radio system, an antenna, and a requirement to establish communications with a distant station.
standard: Orient the antenna to match the polarization of the electric field to achieve maximum signal pickup per MCRP 3-40.3C.
performanceSteps: Determine the polarization of the transmitting station (vertical or horizontal).
For vertical polarization, orient the antenna elements at right angles to the Earth's surface.
For horizontal polarization, orient the antenna elements parallel to the Earth's surface.
Adjust orientation for maximum signal voltage (pickup) at the receiver.
Monitor for elliptical polarization if the field rotates through space, adjusting for both horizontal and vertical components.

title: Mitigate Manmade Noise Interference
condition: Given a radio system experiencing interference from manmade sources such as power lines, vehicles, or electronic equipment.
standard: Reduce interference to achieve a reliable signal-to-noise ratio that allows for clear communication per MCRP 3-40.3C.
performanceSteps: Identify potential sources of manmade noise (e.g., automobile ignition, power lines, fluorescent lights).
Relocate the receiving system at least one kilometer away from the noise source if tactical situation permits.
Orient the receiving antenna for horizontal polarization to exploit the vertical polarization of noise waves near the source.
Balance the antenna and transmission line with respect to the ground to cancel noise voltages.
Utilize a narrowband antenna to reject strong interfering signals near the desired frequency.
Deactivate non-essential electronic equipment in the immediate vicinity.

title: Select Antenna Based on Frequency and Range
condition: Given a mission requirement, an assigned frequency (HF, VHF, or UHF), and a specified range.
standard: Select an antenna configuration that supports the assigned frequency band and range requirements per MCRP 3-40.3C.
performanceSteps: Identify the assigned frequency band (HF, VHF, or UHF).
Select HF antennas for long-range communications requirements.
Select VHF or UHF antennas for line-of-sight (LOS) communications.
Select a 1.5 meter tuned whip antenna for frequencies below 1 MHz to deliver usable signals in high-noise environments.
Determine the required configuration (manpack, vehicle-mounted, or sheltered) based on mobility requirements.

title: Select Antenna Polarization
condition: Given a tactical radio, a frequency, and a mission requirement.
standard: Select the correct polarization (vertical, horizontal, or circular) based on the frequency band and transmission mode (ground wave, sky wave, or SATCOM) to ensure a reliable communication net per MCRP 3-40.3C.
performanceSteps: Identify the assigned frequency band (HF, VHF, or UHF).
Determine the transmission mode (Ground Wave, Sky Wave, or SATCOM).
Select vertical polarization for ground wave transmission at medium and low frequencies.
Select horizontal or vertical polarization for HF sky wave transmission (preferring horizontal for high-angle radiation).
Match polarization between transmitting and receiving antennas for VHF and UHF line-of-sight communications.
Select circular polarization for satellite communications (SATCOM).
Configure the antenna physically to match the selected polarization.

title: Orient a Directional Antenna
condition: Given a horizontal half-wave antenna, a distant station location, and a requirement to communicate.
standard: Orient the antenna to maximize signal strength to the desired station and minimize interference from undesired stations per MCRP 3-40.3C.
performanceSteps: Identify the azimuth to the receiving station.
Identify the location of any known interfering stations.
Deploy the horizontal half-wave antenna.
Orient the antenna broadside (perpendicular) to the desired receiving station for maximum signal strength.
Point the ends of the antenna toward interfering stations to minimize undesired signals.
Verify communication effectiveness with the distant station.

title: Establish an Antenna Ground
condition: Given a grounded antenna system and grounding materials.
standard: Establish a ground connection with the highest possible conductivity to reduce ground losses and provide a reflecting surface for radiated energy per MCRP 3-40.3C.
performanceSteps: Identify the requirement for a grounded antenna based on frequency (low/medium).
Select a location with high ground conductivity.
Prepare the ground connection point to ensure minimum resistance.
Install the ground stake or grounding system.
Connect the antenna ground lead to the grounding system.
Ensure the connection is secure and free of debris.

title: Employ Tactical Single-Channel Radio (SCR) Antennas
condition: Given a tactical radio, antenna components, and a mission requirement.
standard: Select and employ the appropriate antenna to convert a marginal net into a reliable net by optimizing signal strength at the receiving station per MCRP 3-40.3C.
performanceSteps: Determine the required range (short, medium, or long-range).
Select the appropriate frequency band (HF, VHF, or UHF).
Select the antenna configuration (hand-held, manpack, vehicle-mounted, or sheltered).
Account for environmental factors (terrain, dense forests, or atmospheric interference).
Coordinate timing, frequency, and equipment with the distant station.
Install the antenna according to the selected configuration.

title: Select an Antenna for a Radio Communications Circuit
condition: Given a mission requirement, a specific frequency band (HF, VHF, or UHF), and MCRP 3-40.3C.
standard: To provide the strongest possible signal-to-noise (S/N) ratio at the receiving antenna by matching antenna characteristics to the required propagation path.
performanceSteps: Identify the required frequency band (HF, VHF, or UHF) based on the communication equipment provided.
Determine the required range (Ground Wave vs. Sky Wave) for the mission.
Select an antenna compatible with the frequency range (HF: 2–29.999 MHz, VHF: 30–88 MHz or 116–150 MHz, UHF: 225–400 MHz).
Match the antenna type to the intended propagation path (Ground Wave for short range/LOS, Sky Wave for long range/HF).
Verify the antenna selection supports the required power output (0.5–5 kW for HF, <0.5 kW for VHF/UHF).

title: Establish a Radio Link
condition: Given a transmitter, power supply (battery or generator), transmission lines, transmitting antenna, receiving antenna, and receiver.
standard: To successfully generate, radiate, propagate, intercept, and demodulate a signal so that information is available in a useful form at the receiving station.
performanceSteps: Connect the power supply to the transmitter to provide operating voltage.
Connect the transmission line from the transmitter to the transmitting antenna.
Configure the transmitter to generate a radio signal modulated with information (voice or data).
Radiate the electromagnetic wave via the transmitting antenna into the propagation path.
Intercept the wave using the receiving antenna.
Route the signal through the transmission line to the receiver.
Demodulate the energy at the receiver to retrieve the original information.

title: Configure Radio Propagation Path
condition: Given a tactical Single Channel Radio (SCR) and mission parameters.
standard: To establish a communication path using either ground wave or sky wave propagation based on distance and frequency band requirements.
performanceSteps: Determine the distance to the receiving station.
Select Ground Wave propagation for short-distance, UHF, or upper VHF transmissions.
Select Sky Wave propagation for long-distance transmissions (HF) requiring ionospheric refraction.
For VHF/UHF transmissions, ensure a direct Line of Sight (LOS) exists between the transmitter and receiver.
Adjust transmitter output power based on the propagation medium and band (HF, VHF, or UHF) as specified in Table 1-1.
Orient the antenna to maximize signal strength for the chosen propagation path.

title: Select a Site for an Antenna Farm
condition: Given a tactical requirement, a designated area of operations, and MCRP 3-40.3C.
standard: To ensure maximum signal propagation and minimize interference, accounting for tactical, technical, and doctrinal considerations per MCRP 3-40.3C.
performanceSteps: Analyze doctrinal considerations based on Command Post type (Main, Tactical, or Rear).
Evaluate tactical considerations including cover, concealment, and security.
Assess technical considerations including grounding, interference, and physical obstructions.
Identify specific sites for VHF transmitting antennas.
Identify specific sites for VHF receiving antennas.

title: Select Radio Equipment based on Frequency Band
condition: Given a communication requirement (Range and Environment) and MCRP 3-40.3C.
standard: Select the appropriate frequency band and equipment to meet the range requirement (HF for 0-50 miles ground/100-8000 sky; VHF for 0-30 miles; UHF for 0-50 miles) per Table 1-1.
performanceSteps: Determine the required communication range (Ground Wave vs Sky Wave).
Identify the appropriate frequency band (HF, VHF, or UHF) based on range and propagation characteristics.
Select the corresponding radio set (e.g., AN/PRC-104 for HF, AN/PRC-119 for VHF, AN/PRC-113 for UHF).
Verify Line of Sight (LOS) requirements for VHF and UHF bands.
Confirm power requirements for the selected band.

title: Arrange an Antenna Farm
condition: Given multiple antennas, radio sets, and MCRP 3-40.3C.
standard: Arrange the internal components of the antenna farm to ensure electromagnetic compatibility and signal integrity per the layout principles in MCRP 3-40.3C.
performanceSteps: Select antennas based on frequency band requirements.
Determine optimal placement for each antenna to minimize cosite interference.
Establish correct polarization (Vertical or Horizontal) for the circuit.
Route power and signal lines to prevent interference and tripping hazards.
Apply antenna farm layout principles to the physical site.

title: Employ an AS-2259/GR Antenna
condition: Given an HF radio, AS-2259/GR antenna kit, and a requirement to establish Near Vertical Incidence Skywave (NVIS) communications.
standard: Assemble and erect the antenna to establish communications in accordance with MCRP 3-40.3C.
performanceSteps: Inventory all antenna components for completeness.
Assemble the mast sections to the required height.
Attach the top cap and radiating elements.
Deploy guy wires and stakes at 90-degree intervals.
Connect the antenna feed line to the radio set.
Verify signal strength and adjust for NVIS optimization.

title: Construct a Field Expedient Half-Wave Dipole Antenna
condition: Given a frequency, copper wire, insulators, feed line (coaxial or twin-lead), and support structures.
standard: Construct and erect the antenna to achieve a functional communication link per the calculated frequency requirements in MCRP 3-40.3C.
performanceSteps: Calculate the length of the antenna using the formula (468 / frequency in MHz).
Cut the wire into two equal lengths for the dipole halves.
Attach the center insulator and end insulators.
Connect the feed line to the center insulator.
Hoist the antenna to the desired height using support structures.
Connect the feed line to the transmitter/receiver.

title: Establish an Antenna Ground System
condition: Given a radio system, ground rods, ground leads, and a site with low soil conductivity.
standard: Install a ground connection that minimizes resistance to provide an effective reflecting surface per MCRP 3-40.3C.
performanceSteps: Select a location for the ground rod near the antenna base.
Drive the ground rod (or expedient bayonet) into the soil.
Connect the ground lead from the equipment to the rod using a secure clamp.
Treat the soil with conductive substances (e.g., sodium chloride or magnesium sulfate) if resistance remains high.
Ensure the ground lead is as short and direct as possible.

title: Perform Field Repair of Wire Antennas
condition: Given a damaged wire antenna, splicing materials, and hand tools.
standard: Restore the electrical continuity of the antenna to support mission requirements per MCRP 3-40.3C.
performanceSteps: Identify the break or point of damage in the antenna wire.
Strip the insulation from the ends of the broken wire.
Splice the wires together using a secure mechanical connection (e.g., Western Union splice).
Seal the connection to prevent corrosion or further damage.
Re-tension the antenna wire and verify continuity.

title: Integrate a Balun into an Antenna System
condition: Given a balanced antenna, an unbalanced transmitter output, and a balun (balanced-to-unbalanced transformer).
standard: Install the balun to transform energy between balanced and unbalanced circuits to reduce noise and improve signal quality per MCRP 3-40.3C.
performanceSteps: Determine the placement of the balun (at the antenna terminals or the transmitter).
Connect the balanced antenna leads to the balanced side of the balun.
Connect the coaxial transmission line to the unbalanced side of the balun.
Secure all connections and weather-proof if located at the antenna.
Verify the reduction of manmade noise or interference in the system.

title: Determine Antenna Polarization Requirements
condition: Given a mission requirement, a tactical radio, and a specific frequency band (LF, MF, HF, VHF, or UHF).
standard: To ensure the transmitting and receiving antennas are oriented to provide the strongest possible signal and minimize loss per MCRP 6-22D.
performanceSteps: Identify the operating frequency band (LF, MF, HF, VHF, or UHF).
Determine the propagation mode (Ground Wave or Sky Wave).
Select vertical polarization for LF or MF ground wave transmissions to prevent shorting out horizontal lines of force.
Select horizontal or vertical polarization for HF sky wave transmissions based on directional requirements.
Match polarization (horizontal-to-horizontal or vertical-to-vertical) for VHF and UHF line-of-sight transmissions.
Orient the antenna to maintain the original polarization produced at the transmitting station.

title: Analyze Ionospheric Effects on Communications
condition: Given a High Frequency (HF) radio net and observed signal degradation or loss.
standard: Identify the specific ionospheric variation affecting the circuit and determine the impact on the communication link per MCRP 6-22D.
performanceSteps: Monitor for Sudden Ionospheric Disturbance (SID) indicated by total absorption of frequencies above 1 MHz during daylight hours.
Identify Ionospheric Storms characterized by rapid blasting and fading (flutter fading) above 1.5 MHz.
Detect Sporadic E effects causing unexpected long-range propagation or blanking of higher layer reflections.
Assess sunspot activity levels to determine usability of frequencies above 20 MHz.
Adjust operating frequencies or transmission times to compensate for regular and irregular ionospheric variations.

title: Establish Sky Wave Transmission Paths
condition: Given a tactical radio, an antenna, and a requirement for long-distance communication.
standard: Determine the necessary frequency and angle of incidence to ensure the signal reflects off the ionosphere to the target skip distance per MCRP 6-22D.
performanceSteps: Determine the ionization density of the target ionospheric layer (E or F).
Identify the critical frequency for the ionized layer.
Select an operating frequency below the critical frequency for vertical transmissions or adjust the angle of incidence for higher frequencies.
Calculate the critical angle to ensure the radio wave is reflected back to Earth rather than passing into space.
Adjust the antenna angle of transmission to meet the required skip distance for the receiving station.

title: Determine Operating Frequency for Sky Wave Propagation
condition: Given a mission requirement, a high frequency (HF) radio, and current ionospheric conditions.
standard: Select a frequency that is below the critical frequency and above the absorption level of the D-layer to ensure reflection back to Earth, in accordance with MCRP 6-22D.
performanceSteps: Analyze ionospheric layers (D, E, F) based on time of day and solar activity.
Identify the critical frequency for the current ionization density.
Select an operating frequency below the critical frequency for the intended path.
Adjust frequency selection based on sunspot activity levels to ensure reflection.
Monitor for Sudden Ionospheric Disturbances (SID) that may require frequency shifts.

title: Adjust Antenna Height for Signal Coverage
condition: Given a tactical radio, a field-expedient or standard antenna, and a specified communication range requirement.
standard: Adjust the antenna height to control the angle of incidence to either achieve Near-Vertical Incidence Skywave (NVIS) for short-range or low-angle radiation for long-range, ensuring the skip zone does not interfere with the target area.
performanceSteps: Determine the required communication range (short-range vs. long-distance).
Identify the desired angle of incidence for the signal path.
Lower antenna height to increase the angle of transmission for broad, even signal patterns (NVIS).
Raise antenna height to lower the angle of incidence for long-distance communication paths.
Verify the absence of an undesirable skip zone between the ground wave and the first sky wave return point.

title: Troubleshoot HF Signal Degradation
condition: Operating an HF radio net and experiencing irregular signal variations or fading.
standard: Identify the cause of signal degradation and apply appropriate frequency or antenna management techniques to maintain the communication link.
performanceSteps: Monitor the receiver for signs of signal degradation (e.g., flutter fading, total absorption).
Differentiate between regular variations and irregular variations (Sporadic E, SID, or Ionospheric Storms).
Identify Sudden Ionospheric Disturbances (SID) by checking for total absorption above 1 MHz during daylight hours.
Identify Ionospheric Storms by the presence of rapid blasting and fading (flutter fading).
Adjust operating frequency or transmission hops to compensate for atmospheric interference.
Report ionospheric status to the Net Control Station (NCS) if communications are blanked out.

title: Orient a Directional Antenna using a Magnetic Compass
condition: Given a directional antenna, a magnetic compass, a map of magnetic declination, and a target azimuth for the radio path.
standard: Align the antenna to the true azimuth of the radio path within +/- 10 degrees (or as specified by the antenna's beamwidth) to ensure maximum signal strength and minimize radiation pattern error.
performanceSteps: Determine the azimuth of the radio path.
Consult the magnetic declination map to identify the variation of the compass needle from true north for the current location.
Adjust the compass reading to account for magnetic declination to determine true north.
Align the antenna's primary radiation lobe along the calculated true azimuth.
Erect the antenna securely to maintain the correct azimuth.

title: Troubleshoot Marginal Communications
condition: Given a radio circuit experiencing marginal signal quality, necessary tools (tape, wrenches), and operational equipment.
standard: Improve communication quality by performing systematic technical adjustments until signal strength is optimized or restored to operational standards.
performanceSteps: Check, tighten, and tape all cable couplings and connections.
Retune all transmitters and receivers in the circuit.
Verify that the antennas are adjusted for the proper operating frequency.
Adjust the heights of the antennas to improve signal path.
Relocate the antenna a short distance away from its original location to find a better signal spot.
Separate transmitters from receiving equipment if feasible to reduce interference.

title: Match Impedance by Optimizing Transmission Line Length
condition: Given a transceiver (50-ohm internal impedance), a transmission line with mismatched impedance, a load antenna, and a single operating frequency.
standard: Cut the transmission line to a specific length (half-wavelength or quarter-wavelength) to achieve maximum energy transfer and minimize reflected energy.
performanceSteps: Identify the impedance of the transceiver, transmission line, and antenna.
Determine the operating frequency for the circuit.
Calculate the physical length of a half-wavelength or quarter-wavelength for the specific frequency.
Cut the transmission line to the calculated length (or a multiple of half-wavelengths) to repeat the receiver impedance at the antenna connection.
For end-fed long-wire antennas, cut the wire to include a quarter-wavelength section to serve as the matching transmission line.
Connect the optimized line to the transmitter and antenna and verify the match.

title: Establish a Radio Communications Circuit
condition: Given a tactical Single Channel Radio (SCR), power supply, transmission lines, antennas, and a distant station.
standard: Establish a radio link that provides the greatest signal-to-noise (S/N) ratio at the receiving antenna, ensuring information is available in a useful form per MCRP 3-40.3C.
performanceSteps: Generate and radiate an electromagnetic wave modulated with information (e.g., voice, Morse code).
Propagate the wave efficiently from the transmitting antenna to the receiving antenna by matching antenna characteristics to the propagation path.
Intercept the wave by using a receiving antenna.
Demodulate the energy so that the information originally transmitted becomes available in a useful form.

title: Select Frequency Band for Tactical Communications
condition: Given a mission requirement with specific range and terrain constraints.
standard: Select the frequency band (HF, VHF, or UHF) and corresponding equipment that meets range requirements and accounts for Line of Sight (LOS) obstructions per Table 1-1 and 1-2.
performanceSteps: Determine the required range for the communication link (Ground Wave vs. Sky Wave).
Assess Line of Sight (LOS) requirements and identify massive obstructions for VHF/UHF paths.
Select HF for long-range communications (100–8000 miles sky wave).
Select VHF for short-range communications (0–30 miles ground wave) when LOS is available.
Select UHF for critical LOS (ground to air) or SATCOM requirements.
Identify the appropriate MAGTF SCR equipment for the selected band (e.g., AN/PRC-104 for HF, AN/PRC-119 for VHF, or AN/PSC-5 for UHF SATCOM).

title: Account for Ground Wave Propagation Factors
condition: Operating a radio circuit using ground wave propagation over varying terrain.
standard: Adjust frequency and antenna height to overcome surface absorption and Earth's curvature to maintain the radio link.
performanceSteps: Identify the Earth's surface conductivity for the transmission path (e.g., Ocean, Loamy Soil, or Jungle).
Select lower frequencies (below 10 MHz) to utilize the surface wave component when conductivity is high.
Increase transmitting or receiving antenna height to extend the Direct Wave Line of Sight (LOS) distance.
Monitor for signal cancellation caused by ground reflected waves arriving 180 degrees out of phase.
Adjust transmitter power output to compensate for signal absorption in poor conductivity environments like desert or jungle.

title: Utilize Sky Wave Propagation
condition: Given a requirement for long-distance communications beyond the horizon.
standard: Establish a communication path using ionospheric refraction to bridge distances between 50 and 8000 miles.
performanceSteps: Select a frequency within the HF (2–29.999 MHz) or VHF (30–88 MHz) band suitable for sky wave refraction.
Identify the current ionospheric layers (D, E, F1, F2) based on time of day.
Account for the merging of F1 and F2 layers into a single F layer at night.
Account for the fading of D and E layers during night operations.
Orient the antenna to direct the signal toward the ionosphere for refraction back to Earth.

title: Select Radio Frequency Band based on Mission Requirements
condition: Given a mission requirement specifying range and environment, and MCRP 6-22D (Antenna Handbook).
standard: Select the appropriate frequency band (HF, VHF, or UHF) to meet the range and propagation requirements as defined in Table 1-1 and Table 1-2 of the reference.
performanceSteps: Identify the required communication range (Ground Wave vs. Sky Wave).
Determine if Line of Sight (LOS) is achievable for the terrain.
Select the High Frequency (HF) band for long-range (100-8000 miles) sky wave or 0-50 miles ground wave.
Select the Very High Frequency (VHF) band for short-range (0-30 miles) LOS communications.
Select the Ultrahigh Frequency (UHF) band for critical LOS (ground-to-air) or SATCOM requirements.
Identify the specific Single Channel Radio (SCR) equipment required for the selected band.

title: Configure Antenna for Near-Vertical Incidence Skywave (NVIS) Propagation
condition: Given an HF radio system, antenna components, and a requirement for short-range skywave communication (avoiding a skip zone).
standard: Adjust antenna height to increase the angle of incidence, providing broad signal coverage in a large area without a skip zone, in accordance with MCRP 6-22D.
performanceSteps: Determine the desired coverage area and operating frequency.
Calculate the appropriate antenna height relative to the operating frequency.
Lower the antenna height to increase the angle of transmission (Angle of Incidence).
Verify the elimination of the skip zone (the area between ground wave and sky wave return).
Establish communication with the receiving station using the NVIS path.

title: Identify Components of a Radio Communication Link
condition: Given a tactical radio system and MCRP 6-22D.
standard: Identify all seven discrete components of a radio link to ensure system integrity and troubleshooting capability.
performanceSteps: Identify the Transmitter.
Identify the Power Supply.
Identify the Transmission Lines.
Identify the Transmitting Antenna.
Identify the Propagation Path.
Identify the Receiving Antenna.
Identify the Receiver.

title: Mitigate Signal Fading in HF Communications
condition: Given an HF radio circuit experiencing periodic fluctuations in received signal strength.
standard: Implement mitigation techniques to maintain a reliable receiving signal above the background noise level without relying solely on increased transmitter power.
performanceSteps: Monitor the received signal for periodic increases and decreases in strength.
Analyze the signal-to-noise ratio to determine if the fade is below background noise.
Select the correct operating frequency based on atmospheric conditions (MUF/LUF).
Adjust antenna gain or orientation to optimize signal reception.
Verify circuit reliability and signal strength at the receiving station.

title: Select an Antenna for Single-Channel Radio (SCR) Operations
condition: Given a mission requirement, a tactical radio, and MCRP 3-40.3C.
standard: To provide the strongest possible signal at the receiving station of the circuit based on the military radio frequency band (HF, VHF, or UHF) and operational environment.
performanceSteps: Identify the required military radio frequency band (HF, VHF, or UHF).
Determine the required range and mode of operation (simplex or half-duplex).
Account for environmental factors including terrain and atmospheric interference.
Select the antenna configuration (hand-held, manpack, vehicle-mounted, bench-mounted, or sheltered) that optimizes signal strength.

title: Employ Single-Channel Radio (SCR) Jam Resistance and COMSEC
condition: Given a tactical radio, common timing, frequency data, and mission requirements.
standard: To establish secure voice communication and jam resistance through frequency hopping while minimizing susceptibility to enemy electronic warfare.
performanceSteps: Ensure common timing is established between stations.
Verify common frequency and equipment compatibility.
Enable integrated communications security (COMSEC) for secure voice and data exchange.
Activate frequency hopping mode to provide jam resistance.

title: Employ SCR Satellite Communications (SATCOM)
condition: Given a tactical radio with SATCOM capability and limited spectrum availability.
standard: To provide mobile, flexible communications with unlimited range while coordinating for limited spectrum availability.
performanceSteps: Coordinate for spectrum availability and frequency assignment.
Configure the SCR equipment for SATCOM mode.
Establish communication link to provide mobility and flexibility in the MAGTF CIS architecture.
Monitor the link for interference or footprint limitations.
